headline: High: ms-swift can write/egress by default while the paired repo is a non-runnable docs-only content source, creating leakage and conflict risks if wired together.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A is a docs-only content-writing repo with no runnable I/O surfaces, so it cannot itself ingest B’s outputs by default. B can read/write files and process stdin/stdout, so if an operator manually bridges A’s content into B, prompt injection is possible, but the pathway is not default and blast radius is limited.
conditions: IF an operator copies A-generated text into B’s stdin or files, B may follow injected instructions.
IF B is configured to treat repository text as trusted prompts, injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Do not paste A outputs into B without sanitizing instructions.
Add a fixed system prompt that ignores repository-authored directives.
Use a review step before B consumes any A-produced text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no I/O surfaces, but B reads and writes files, handles secrets, and calls external APIs. If A and B share a workspace or files, B can ingest and transmit A-associated contents. The pairwise leakage path exists in default CLI/file workflows, though A alone is not sensitive.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or training workspace, B can read A-produced files.
IF B processes those files through allowlisted egress, contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Place A and B in separate directories.
Disable B network egress for runs that touch shared files.
Avoid storing secrets in any shared workspace.
Use read-only mounts for A artifacts.
Review B logs for accidental content capture.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network capabilities, while B can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. There is no direct write-write conflict from A, but if A’s artifacts are placed in B’s writable workspace, B can overwrite or mutate them. Uncertainty about shared-state isolation pushes this above low.
conditions: IF A artifacts are stored in a directory writable by B, B can modify them.
IF the orchestrator lacks locking, concurrent B instances may race on shared files.
mitigations: Use separate output directories per agent.
Mount A artifacts read-only for B.
Disable concurrent B runs on the same workspace.
Add file locks around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a content-writing source and B can act on files and shell commands, so A’s output can become B’s input without a verification gate. B’s support-style workflow and API/file access make it plausible that it treats upstream text as authoritative. This is a default pipeline risk, though not inherently irreversible.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text as instructions or facts, downstream actions may follow incorrect content.
IF B is allowed to execute shell commands from parsed text, errors can cascade into system changes.
mitigations: Insert a human verification step before B acts on A output.
Require structured schemas for A-to-B handoff.
Block shell execution on untrusted text.
Log and diff A outputs before B consumes them.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A, and B’s profile only shows generic docs-only evidence plus secret handling. Because the pair lacks explicit compliance metadata, only a weak compliance concern is supportable. A is not cited for a specific violation beyond being a docs-only repo; B’s secret handling is the only concrete compliance-relevant surface.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s secret-handling workflows, retention and access controls must be reviewed.
IF A is repurposed to store jurisdiction-bound content, residency policy must be checked.
mitigations: Confirm whether regulated data enters B.
Review B retention settings before use.
Keep secrets out of shared artifacts.
Document the data flow for any compliance review.
